brief.paper_summary:
由于现实世界中的大多数数据都可以用图表示，因此近年来针对图表示学
习的研究越来越受到关注。通过将高维图数据转化成低维的表征向量，图表示
学习可以有效地对图的信息进行存储并快捷地访问图中实体的关键知识。利用
学习到的图表征数据可以为社交网络行为分析、节点分类、链路预测和聚类等
下游任务提供帮助。随着深度学习的快速发展，研究人员提出了基于图神经网
络的图表示学习方法，其使图中的节点能够同时学习图的结构信息以及邻域节
点的特征信息，从而得到高质量的低维表征。针对图神经网络上的图表示学
习，本文主要关注两个问题：大规模时序图场景下的图表示学习方法和分布式
场景下的大规模图的图神经网络优化训练方法。
真实世界中的图数据规模往往十分庞大且处于动态变化的状态，而现有的
图神经网络要么无法处理动态时序图上的图表征学习，要么面对大规模图数据
集时训练效率低下。为了解决大规模动态图上的图表征学习问题，本文提出了
一种基于图摘要的大规模时序图表示学习方法——GSAERU 模型。GSAERU 模
型由“图表征学习模块”和“时序学习模块”两部分构成。首先将动态时序图
建模为各时刻上原图快照的序列，接着在单时间步上将图快照输入图表征学习
模块。该模块通过图摘要技术对原图进行压缩，并将压缩后的新图输入图自编
码器，利用和原图的重构误差训练原图节点的表征。在获得单时间步上的图表
征后将其输入时序学习模块，并通过一个循环神经网络学习原图在时间维度上
的特征信息与依赖关系，从而得到大规模时序图的高质量表征。基于在四个真
实世界的大规模图数据集上的大量实验表明，GSAERU 模型能够高效生成时序
图的表征。与传统的图神经网络算法相比，其平均内存消耗和平均训练时长只
有其9.86% 与13.27%，且与性能最好的算法在大部分指标下的差距都不超过
3.5%。

ii
使用分布式技术加速神经网络训练也是如今热门的研究课题，因为在处理
大规模数据时，单个设备（如CPU，GPU）有限的内存和计算资源往往会成为
训练瓶颈。而分布式技术可以提供更多的计算资源来提高训练效率。然而由于
图数据的不规则性，传统分布式机器学习方法中的子任务划分和模型训练方法
难以直接应用于图神经网络。针对大规模图流数据场景下的分布式图神经网络
训练优化问题，本文提出了基于图摘要的分布式图神经网络优化训练算法——
DSGNN 模型。DSGNN 模型采用“领导——工作者”工作模式，首先由领导节
点利用一个基于边分割的图流划分算法对原图进行划分并将划分子图分配给各
个工作节点。工作节点随后执行一个基于图摘要技术的小批量训练并将训练结
果通过一个注意力层返回给领导节点，最后由领导节点汇总结果并计算梯度，
并根据梯度同步更新所有计算节点上的模型。基于四个真实世界的大规模图数
据集上的大量实验，结果表明DSGNN 模型可以大大加速GNN 模型的训练，
并且在链路预测任务上的F1 分数显著高于其它分布式图神经网络模型。

paper.english_abstract:
Since most data in the real world can be represented by graphs, research on graph
representation learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. By transforming high-dimensional graph data into low-dimensional vectors, graph representation
learning can store graph information and access key information of the graph effectively. Utilizing the learned graph representation data can benefit downstream tasks
such as social network, node classification and so on. With the development of deep
learning, researchers have proposed a graph representation learning method based on
graph neural network, which enables nodes in the graph to simultaneously learn the
structural information of the graph and the feature information of neighboring nodes,
thereby obtaining high-quality and low-dimensional representations. For graph representation learning on graph neural networks, this paper focuses on two issues: graph
representation learning methods in large-scale sequential graphs and graph neural network optimization training methods for large-scale graphs in distributed scenarios.
The scale of graph in the real world is often large and keeps changing, and the
existing GNN models are either unable to handle graph representation learning on dynamic sequential graphs, or the training efficiency is low on large-scale graph. To solve
the problem of graph representation learning on large-scale dynamic graphs, this paper
proposes a large-scale sequential graph representation learning method based on graph
summarization—GSAERU model. The GSAERU model consists of two parts: ”graph
representation learning module” and ”time sequence learning module”. First, the dynamic sequence graph is modeled as a sequence of snapshots of the original graph at
each moment, and then the graph snapshots are input into the graph representation learning module at a single time step. This module compresses the original graph through

iv
the graph summarization technology, and inputs the compressed new graph into the
graph autoencoder, and uses the reconstruction error with the original graph to train
the representation of the nodes of the original graph. After the graph representation
on a single time step is obtained, it is input into the timing learning module, and the
feature information and dependencies of the original graph in the time dimension are
learned through a recurrent neural network, so as to obtain a high-quality representation of large-scale timing graphs. Extensive experiments on four real-world large-scale
graph datasets show that the GSAERU model can efficiently generate representations
of timing graphs. Compared with the traditional graph neural network algorithm, its average memory consumption and average training time are only 9.86% and 13.27%, and
the gap with the best performing algorithm in most indicators does not exceed 3.5%.
Using distributed technology to accelerate neural network training is also a hot research topic nowadays. The limited memory and computing resources of a single device
often become a training bottleneck when processing large-scale data. Distributed technology can provide more computing resources to improve training efficiency. However, due to the irregularity of graph data, the subtask division and model training
methods in traditional distributed machine learning methods are difficult to be directly
applied to graph neural networks. Aiming at the optimization problem of distributed
graph neural network training in large-scale graph streaming data scenarios, this paper
proposes a distributed graph neural network optimization training algorithm based on
graph summaries——DSGNN model. The DSGNN model adopts the ”leader-worker”
mode. First, the leader divides the original graph using a graph flow partition algorithm based on edge segmentation and assigns the divided subgraphs to each worker.

and return the training results to the leader through an attention layer. Finally, the leader
summarizes the results and calculates the gradient, and synchronously updates the models on all computing nodes according to the gradient. Based on extensive experiments
on four real-world large-scale graph datasets, the results show that the DSGNN model
can greatly accelerate the training of GNN models, and the F1 score on the link prediction task is significantly higher than other distributed graph neural network models.

摘
要
由于现实世界中的大多数数据都可以用图表示，因此近年来针对图表示学
习的研究越来越受到关注。通过将高维图数据转化成低维的表征向量，图表示
学习可以有效地对图的信息进行存储并快捷地访问图中实体的关键知识。利用
学习到的图表征数据可以为社交网络行为分析、节点分类、链路预测和聚类等
下游任务提供帮助。随着深度学习的快速发展，研究人员提出了基于图神经网
络的图表示学习方法，其使图中的节点能够同时学习图的结构信息以及邻域节
点的特征信息，从而得到高质量的低维表征。针对图神经网络上的图表示学
习，本文主要关注两个问题：大规模时序图场景下的图表示学习方法和分布式
场景下的大规模图的图神经网络优化训练方法。
真实世界中的图数据规模往往十分庞大且处于动态变化的状态，而现有的
图神经网络要么无法处理动态时序图上的图表征学习，要么面对大规模图数据
集时训练效率低下。为了解决大规模动态图上的图表征学习问题，本文提出了
一种基于图摘要的大规模时序图表示学习方法——GSAERU 模型。GSAERU 模
型由“图表征学习模块”和“时序学习模块”两部分构成。首先将动态时序图
建模为各时刻上原图快照的序列，接着在单时间步上将图快照输入图表征学习
模块。该模块通过图摘要技术对原图进行压缩，并将压缩后的新图输入图自编
码器，利用和原图的重构误差训练原图节点的表征。在获得单时间步上的图表
征后将其输入时序学习模块，并通过一个循环神经网络学习原图在时间维度上
的特征信息与依赖关系，从而得到大规模时序图的高质量表征。基于在四个真
实世界的大规模图数据集上的大量实验表明，GSAERU 模型能够高效生成时序
图的表征。与传统的图神经网络算法相比，其平均内存消耗和平均训练时长只
有其9.86% 与13.27%，且与性能最好的算法在大部分指标下的差距都不超过
3.5%。

# Page 6
ii
使用分布式技术加速神经网络训练也是如今热门的研究课题，因为在处理
大规模数据时，单个设备（如CPU，GPU）有限的内存和计算资源往往会成为
训练瓶颈。而分布式技术可以提供更多的计算资源来提高训练效率。然而由于
图数据的不规则性，传统分布式机器学习方法中的子任务划分和模型训练方法
难以直接应用于图神经网络。针对大规模图流数据场景下的分布式图神经网络
训练优化问题，本文提出了基于图摘要的分布式图神经网络优化训练算法——
DSGNN 模型。DSGNN 模型采用“领导——工作者”工作模式，首先由领导节
点利用一个基于边分割的图流划分算法对原图进行划分并将划分子图分配给各
个工作节点。工作节点随后执行一个基于图摘要技术的小批量训练并将训练结
果通过一个注意力层返回给领导节点，最后由领导节点汇总结果并计算梯度，
并根据梯度同步更新所有计算节点上的模型。基于四个真实世界的大规模图数
据集上的大量实验，结果表明DSGNN 模型可以大大加速GNN 模型的训练，
并且在链路预测任务上的F1 分数显著高于其它分布式图神经网络模型。

Abstract
Since most data in the real world can be represented by graphs, research on graph
representation learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. By transforming high-dimensional graph data into low-dimensional vectors, graph representation
learning can store graph information and access key information of the graph effectively. Utilizing the learned graph representation data can benefit downstream tasks
such as social network, node classification and so on. With the development of deep
learning, researchers have proposed a graph representation learning method based on
graph neural network, which enables nodes in the graph to simultaneously learn the
structural information of the graph and the feature information of neighboring nodes,
thereby obtaining high-quality and low-dimensional representations. For graph representation learning on graph neural networks, this paper focuses on two issues: graph
representation learning methods in large-scale sequential graphs and graph neural network optimization training methods for large-scale graphs in distributed scenarios.
The scale of graph in the real world is often large and keeps changing, and the
existing GNN models are either unable to handle graph representation learning on dynamic sequential graphs, or the training efficiency is low on large-scale graph. To solve
the problem of graph representation learning on large-scale dynamic graphs, this paper
proposes a large-scale sequential graph representation learning method based on graph
summarization—GSAERU model. The GSAERU model consists of two parts: ”graph
representation learning module” and ”time sequence learning module”. First, the dynamic sequence graph is modeled as a sequence of snapshots of the original graph at
each moment, and then the graph snapshots are input into the graph representation learning module at a single time step. This module compresses the original graph through

the graph summarization technology, and inputs the compressed new graph into the
graph autoencoder, and uses the reconstruction error with the original graph to train
the representation of the nodes of the original graph. After the graph representation
on a single time step is obtained, it is input into the timing learning module, and the
feature information and dependencies of the original graph in the time dimension are

大规模时序图表示学习的效率问题
在大规模时序图表示学习任务中，主流的解决方法是使用图神经网络与循
环神经网络相结合的框架。首先利用图神经网络学习单时间步上的图表征，接
着将这些表征输入循环神经网络中进行训练以学习其时间维度上的特征。然
而，无论是图神经网络还是卷积神经网络的训练都涉及大量的矩阵乘积计算，

场景中图中节点可能会产生增减，造成前后时间步之间数据规模的变化，使得
循环神经网络无法正常训练。
在大规模时序图中进行图表示学习，同时解决模型训练效率问题，具有如

• 如何对动态图进行建模，使得其能刻画图中节点与边随时间变化的动态过

• 如何在不过分损失模型精度的情况下尽可能缩短模型的训练时间和节约训

分布式场景下的图神经网络训练问题
分布式图神经网络训练的工作流程一般分为三个阶段：1）数据划分；2）
GNN 模型优化；3）梯度聚合。其中梯度聚合步骤的过程与传统分布式机器学
习方法类似，而前两个过程由于图数据分布的不规律性，在实际实施过程中需
要考虑负载均衡，通信开销等具体问题。因此如何在分布式场景下高效训练图
神经网络模型具有如下挑战：
• 如何进行数据分区。数据分区是将输入数据（图和特征）分配到一组工作
节点中。首先考虑到负载均衡问题，每个工作节点应当接收到规模均匀的
子任务从而确保系统不会被某些节点拖慢整体训练速度，而图数据由于节
点分布的不规律性，难以像传统数据一样直接进行划分。此外，GNN 模型
训练时需要不断聚合目标节点的邻域信息，但在分布式场景中其邻域节点
往往会出现本地缺失的现象。如果忽视了这部分缺失的节点，模型的准确
性将会被破坏，如果需要获取目标节点的完整邻域信息，则需要向其它机
器发送请求，造成大量的通信开销，从而降低分布式训练的效率。
• 如何进行本地GNN 模型训练。由于数据的依赖性，工作节点进行本地模型
训练的方式与传统的深度学习训练方法有很大不同。在不访问其他工作节
点获取邻域信息的情况下，可能无法生成正确的计算图从而使得模型的精
度下降。如果采取允许访问其他工作节点的模式，又会带来通信协议选择
和隐藏层之间参数同步的问题。

近几年来，针对时序图上的动态图表示学习问题引起了科研人员的兴趣。
现有的针对时序图的表示学习方法大多是由静态图上的方法拓展而来。
一种流行的动态图表示学习方法是将动态图中节点和边随时间的变化建模

边随时间的增减建模为点过程函数，并使用神经网络将点过程函数参数化，从

从一对节点不连接的状态发展到任意节点两两连接的状态。模型基于所有的三
元闭包过程学习图中节点的表示。HTNE[24] 同样对节点的点过程进行建模，

模为以时间为参数的连续点过程函数，使得模型能够有效生成动态图的表示并

2 . 1 . 3
基于分布式的方法
利用图神经网络进行图表示学习可以得到高质量的表示，但随着图规模的
增大，其消耗的训练时间也急速增长。为了达到加速训练的目的，科研人员尝
试将分布式技术与图神经网络结合，并产出了许多优秀的成果，目前主流的分
布式图神经网络算法可以分为一下四类：
分布式全批量训练中分派子图方法：此类方法在每轮训练中对完整原图进
行训练。首先将图数据和待训练的GNN 模型输入领导节点，在训练过程中领
导节点根据具体的节点特征聚合任务分发给各个工作者节点进行计算，然后收
集返回结果并根据损失函数计算梯度，进行模型参数更新。NeuGraph[28] 通过
将每个顶点的特征平均分成多个部分来探索特征级并行性，从而以更细粒度的
方式划分工作负载。然后将其分配给不同的GPU 线程进行相应的计算。该方法
充分利用了GPU 海量的并行计算资源。ROC[29] 将GPU 内存管理转化为一个
成本最小化问题，它使用递归动态规划算法寻找全局最优解来决定每一块数据
应该缓存在哪个GPU 内存中以供重用。然而，由于只有领导节点保存模型参数
且训练时严重依赖于工作者节点的计算结果，导致这类方法的数据通信开销往
往很大，且每轮训练的运行时间呈现不规律性。
分布式全批量预处理子图划分方法：此类方法也是在每轮训练中使用对
完整原图进行训练，在得到输入的图数据和GNN 模型后，增加了预处理阶段
使领导节点将图提前进行划分，并将每个划分后的子图和一份GNN 模型的副
本发送给对应的工作者节点，由它们在本地进行GNN 模型的训练，最后将结
果返回领导节点，由领导节点汇总后再统一通知工作者节点更新模型参数。
DGCL[30] 分布式GNN 训练提供了一个通用且高效的通信库。它将最短路径
生成树算法运用到传输规划中，通过“避免竞争”的策略提高链路使用效率并
平衡不同链路上的工作负载。FlexGraph[31] 通过合并位于同一分区的相邻顶点
的特征以减少数据传输量。当每个计算节点收到来自其他节点的邻居信息请求
时，首先会在本地聚合部分邻居信息，然后将部分结果发送给请求计算节点，
而不是直接发送初始邻居信息。请求计算节点只需要将接收到的部分结果与其
本地节点进行聚合即可继续计算，这使得通信开销显著减少。然而，这类设计

第一，到目前为止，大部分的GNN 模型是针对不随时间变化的静态图开

基于在真实世界中的大规模时序图数据集上的大量实验，GSAERU 在加速训练
图神经网络训练和维持模型精度方面取得了突出的成绩。

内核（Computation Core）[73, 74]，用于加速图数据计算的编程模型[75, 76]。
然而，这些优化仅仅局限于在单个机器上训练GNN，没有考虑到模型的可扩

如今，真实世界中的网络图规模往往会非常巨大，以社交网络图（微博，

第五章
总结与展望
5 . 1
工作总结
本文着力于目前图表征学习领域存在的两大问题——“大规模图数据训练
耗时耗资源”与“传统方法难以训练动态图”。本文首先概述了图表示学习领
域的相关背景知识，随后对待研究的问题进行了介绍，并对目前针对大规模动
态图表示学习的研究工作和算法进行了整理。基于对当前研究工作中的优势与
缺陷的分析，我们设计了两种算法——“基于图摘要的大规模时序图表示学习
算法”与“基于图摘要的分布式图神经网络训练优化方法”。通过在多个真实
世界的大规模动态图数据集上进行了大量实验，我们验证了算法在加速模型训
练和减少计算资源损耗上的有效性。
对于“大规模图数据难以训练”的问题，本文首先调研了相关的解决方
法，发现现有的解决方法主要围绕两个方面展开：第一，使用采样技术从大规
模图中采集出一个规模远小于原图的子图并在其上进行模型训练，达到加速的
目的；第二，使用分布式技术，通过增加计算节点的数量来加快训练速度。然
而现有方法仍存在一些缺陷。对于采样方法，采样出的子图可能会丢失大量原
图的拓扑信息从而导致模型性能的降低，以及采样生成子图的过程是否可以在
线性时间内完成。对于分布式方法，分布在不同机器上的邻居节点想要获取对
方信息需要发起请求，过多的通信开销会给系统带来极大的负担从而拖慢训练
的速度。因此我们分别提出了基于图摘要的大规模时序图表征学习算法和分布
式图神经网络训练加速算法，通过图摘要技术中的局部敏感哈希对原图中的节
点进行映射从而得到一组规模远小于原图的图摘要。并通过在这些图摘要中
使用时序学习方法与分布式技术达到加速模型训练和减少计算资源消耗的目
的。通过在多个真实世界中的大规模图数据集上进行的实验显示了该方法的有
效性。
对于“传统图表示学习方法难以学习动态图”的问题，本文首先调研了动
态图表示学习的相关工作，发现现有的方法大多使用图神经网络与循环神经网
络相结合的方式来学习动态图的表示，随后我们总结了这类方法的通用框架。

58
第五章
总结与展望
然而在实际应用中，由于循环神经网络的结构特殊性，其要求图中节点不能出
现增减的变化，这就对动态图中节点增减这一情景做出了限制。因此我们提出
了基于图摘要的动态图表示学习方法，其将原图节点通过一个局部敏感哈希映
射到一个规模固定的新图中并学习新图的表示，最后将新图的表示作为循环神
经网络的输入进行时序特征的学习，解决了现有方法无法处理动态图中节点变
化的问题。大量基于真实世界大规模图数据集上的实验表明，本算法可以有效
处理动态图中的时序信息。
5 . 2
前景展望
近年来图表示学习在现实中的多个领域都已取得了引人注目的成绩，包括
金融、生物医学、社交网络，成为了解决链路预测、节点分类问题的有效方
法。然而，随着所研究图的规模日益增大，面对动辄数百万节点与上千万条边
组成的大规模图，传统的图表示学习方法往往不能有效对其进行训练，而引入
采样等技术对原图进行“压缩”后训练的方法又会不可避免地丢失原图拓扑信
息，从而使模型的精度下降。如何找到“效率”与“精度”之间的平衡点仍然
是一个值得研究的问题。
尽管针对图表示学习已经提出了许多有效的方法，但如何提高所学习到表
征的可解释性，即“如何判断训练得到的表征中每一维度特征所包含的具体信
息”仍然是一项具有挑战性的任务。
此外，本文的研究只针对图中节点级的表示学习，而没有对边级别的表征
乃至图级别的表征进行探索。在未来的研究中，将表示学习的范围扩大到针对
边乃至子图可能是一个可行的研究方向。

read_results.text: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks on directed heterogeneous graphs face two structural challenges: symmetric graph aggregations cannot distinguish directional propagation mechanisms, and pure likelihood-based density scoring can underweight sparse localized perturbations. We address both within DA-GTNF, a unified framework for freeway anomaly detection. First, a direction-aware heterogeneous graph explicitly encodes four asymmetric relation types (downstream propagation, upstream shockwave, lateral lane interaction, and diagonal lane change), enabling a Relational GCN to learn independent aggregation kernels per relation. Second, a DualBranchGating mechanism fuses spatial graph embeddings and temporal Transformer embeddings through adaptive, feature-wise gates derived from unfused outputs. Third, a Dual-Conditioned Normalizing Flow estimates exact token-wise conditional log-likelihoods of the gated embeddings, while an auxiliary reconstruction head improves sensitivity to micro-level deviations that may be weakly reflected by NLL alone. On FT-AED, DA-GTNF achieves an AUC of 0.7218, a Reporting Delay of −11.80 min, a Mean Localization Error of 2.23 miles, and 100% incident coverage. On PeMS with incomplete ground truth, the segment-level DA-GTNF variant also consistently improves Recall@K% over all compared baselines.

Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) commonly utilize attention mechanisms to capture spatio-temporal dependencies. However, these methods often derive attention weights based on feature similarity, leading to an insufficient utilization of explicit topological evolution signals. This limitation hinders the model’s ability to perceive distinct structural roles within evolving graphs. To address this issue, we introduce Knowledge-Enhanced Spatio-Temporal ModuleKESTM (KES TM), a unified framework that bridges lightweight structural priors with adaptive spatio-temporal attention. KESTM comprises three key components: (1) a Knowledge Enhancement Module (KEM) that encodes multi-scale degree statistics and structural embeddings into learnable node-level priors; (2) an Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Encoder (ASTE) that employs a dual-stream attention mechanism with sparsity-aware gating to dynamically balance structural and temporal signals; and (3) a Dynamic Temporal-Contrastive Loss (DTCL) that jointly handles class imbalance and temporal inconsistency. Extensive experiments on four real-world dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. In particular, KESTM shows significant robustness under extreme graph sparsity, effectively addressing the Sparsity-Performance Paradox. Code is available at https://github.com/tyut2018/KESTM .

Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting still suffers from three linked limitations: balanced graph operators mismatch open road networks, sequence-style SSMs ignore real graph topology, and physics losses may become self-referential. We propose UOT-GraphSSM, which combines an unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) layer, a graph-native anisotropic SSM recurrence, and a stop-gradient CTM physics loss. The UOT layer produces a mass-relaxed asymmetric transport plan for directional boundary flux; the GraphSSM recurrence propagates hidden states along this plan rather than along a serialized node order; and the CTM loss provides non-circular physical regularisation. On PEMS04/07/08, UOT-GraphSSM achieves consistent state-of-the-art results, reducing MSE by 7–25%, lowering long-horizon degradation from 65% to 43%, and retaining a compact 1.6 M-parameter footprint.

Among various spatio-temporal prediction tasks, epidemic forecasting plays a critical role in public health management. Recent studies have demonstrated the strong potential of spatio-temporal graph neural networks in extracting heterogeneous spatio-temporal patterns for epidemic forecasting. However, most of these methods bear an oversimplified assumption that two locations (e.g., cities) with similar observed features in previous time steps will develop similar infection numbers in the future. In fact, for any epidemic disease, there exists strong heterogeneity of its latent transmission dynamics across both geolocation and time, which can eventually lead to diverged infection numbers in two “similar” locations. However, capturing such latent transmission heterogeneity is non-trivial due to the existence of numerous influencing factors like medical resource accessibility, virus mutations, mobility patterns, etc., most of which are spatio-temporal yet unreachable or even unobservable. To address this challenge, we propose a Heterogeneous Epidemic-Aware Transmission Graph Neural Network (HeatGNN), a novel epidemic forecasting framework. By integrating epidemiological modeling into a Graph Neural Network, HeatGNN learns epidemiology-informed location embeddings of different locations that reflect their own transmission dynamics over time. On top of the conventional spatio-temporal module, a heterogeneous transmission graph network is designed to uncover the latent transmission heterogeneity among locations, where the time-varying latent transmission affinity graphs are computed on-the-fly and provide additional predictive signals. Experiments (Code is available at https://github.com/YufanZheng/HeatGNN_ECML-PKDD .) on four benchmark datasets have revealed that HeatGNN outperforms various strong baselines.

With the rapid development of IoT technologies and widespread deployment of intelligent sensing devices, dynamic sensor selection has become crucial for balancing recognition accuracy and energy efficiency in applications like health monitoring. Existing runtime assessment methods suffer from limited predictive utility for future sensor quality and fail to capture dynamic spatio-temporal dependencies among interconnected devices. To this end, we propose a utility-aware sensor selection framework that integrates adaptive spatio-temporal forecasting with attention-based quality assessment. Our approach employs a Dynamic Graph Learning-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (DGL-STGCN) to model evolving device correlations and predict sensor states, while an attention mechanism assesses future sensor utility through learned importance scores. This enables proactive sensor selection optimized for both recognition accuracy and energy consumption, explicitly accounting for switching overheads. We develop and evaluate a prototype system designed for wearable devices to monitor locomotion activities. Results show that our system achieves a 14% accuracy improvement over single-sensor baselines, a 25% reduction in energy consumption compared to full-sensor deployment, and a 2% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at equivalent energy levels.

Accurate traffic forecasting requires effective modeling of complex spatio-temporal dependencies and reliable uncertainty estimation. Although existing graph-based methods have achieved strong performance, most focus on deterministic prediction and do not explicitly incorporate structural information into probabilistic modeling. In this paper, we propose HBPC-GWN, a hierarchical Bayesian calibration framework for graph-based traffic forecasting. Rather than imposing structural constraints during training, the proposed method performs posterior-level calibration by integrating a Laplacian-based prior into the predictive distribution. This enables a principled combination of data-driven predictions and graph-structured regularization, improving the consistency between spatial structure and uncertainty estimation. We instantiate the framework on Graph WaveNet and evaluate it on multiple real-world traffic datasets. Experimental results show that HBPC-GWN achieves competitive and more stable performance across forecasting horizons. In particular, it provides consistent improvements in medium- and long-term forecasting and improves probabilistic calibration, as reflected by better negative log-likelihood and prediction interval coverage. These results demonstrate that incorporating structural priors at the posterior level is an effective and flexible strategy for enhancing both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation in traffic forecasting.

Accurate forecasting of electric vehicle (EV) charging demand is essential for maintaining power-grid stability and supporting the efficient operation of urban charging infrastructure. However, EV charging demand exhibits strong spatio-temporal heterogeneity, multi-scale fluctuations, and complex dependencies, making accurate forecasting challenging. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-informed spatio-temporal graph learning framework for EV charging demand forecasting. Specifically, PSO-optimized MVMD is used to reconstruct multi-regional occupancy sequences, while a 2D-CNN is employed to capture temporal interaction patterns between occupancy and electricity price. A GAT-GFC-BiGRU-TPA architecture is then developed to model spatial dependencies and key temporal dynamics across charging regions. In addition, a physics-informed meta-learning strategy with a price-sensitivity regularization term is introduced to better capture the demand-response relationship between charging demand and electricity price while improving cross-region adaptability and training stability. Experiments on a real-world EV charging dataset show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple forecasting horizons. Ablation studies further verify the effectiveness of the major components. Overall, the proposed framework effectively captures complex spatio-temporal dynamics and improves short- and medium-term EV charging demand forecasting.

Multi-type epileptiform events, including spike and ripple activities in electroencephalogram (EEG), are important biomarkers for seizure detection; however, their accurate detection is challenging due to complex spatio-temporal dynamics and multi-scale oscillatory patterns. To address these challenges, we propose a unified framework that integrates clinically motivated multi-band decomposition with dynamic spatio-temporal representation learning for accurate classification of EEG signals. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into multiple frequency branches, followed by a branch-aware wavelet enhancement module to emphasize transient oscillatory patterns. A multi-scale temporal convolution module is then employed to capture diverse temporal dynamics across different time scales. Finally, a dynamic spatio-temporal graph reasoning module constructs sample-adaptive spatial and temporal graphs and performs joint propagation to model inter-channel interactions and temporal dependencies. Extensive experiments conducted on both a private clinical dataset and the public TUEV dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in epileptic event detection. These results highlight its effectiveness in capturing clinically relevant EEG patterns and its potential for assisting automated epilepsy diagnosis.

source_records.abstract: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) commonly utilize attention mechanisms to capture spatio-temporal dependencies. However, these methods often derive attention weights based on feature similarity, leading to an insufficient utilization of explicit topological evolution signals. This limitation hinders the model’s ability to perceive distinct structural roles within evolving graphs. To address this issue, we introduce Knowledge-Enhanced Spatio-Temporal ModuleKESTM (KES TM), a unified framework that bridges lightweight structural priors with adaptive spatio-temporal attention. KESTM comprises three key components: (1) a Knowledge Enhancement Module (KEM) that encodes multi-scale degree statistics and structural embeddings into learnable node-level priors; (2) an Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Encoder (ASTE) that employs a dual-stream attention mechanism with sparsity-aware gating to dynamically balance structural and temporal signals; and (3) a Dynamic Temporal-Contrastive Loss (DTCL) that jointly handles class imbalance and temporal inconsistency. Extensive experiments on four real-world dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. In particular, KESTM shows significant robustness under extreme graph sparsity, effectively addressing the Sparsity-Performance Paradox. Code is available at https://github.com/tyut2018/KESTM .

source_records.abstract: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks on directed heterogeneous graphs face two structural challenges: symmetric graph aggregations cannot distinguish directional propagation mechanisms, and pure likelihood-based density scoring can underweight sparse localized perturbations. We address both within DA-GTNF, a unified framework for freeway anomaly detection. First, a direction-aware heterogeneous graph explicitly encodes four asymmetric relation types (downstream propagation, upstream shockwave, lateral lane interaction, and diagonal lane change), enabling a Relational GCN to learn independent aggregation kernels per relation. Second, a DualBranchGating mechanism fuses spatial graph embeddings and temporal Transformer embeddings through adaptive, feature-wise gates derived from unfused outputs. Third, a Dual-Conditioned Normalizing Flow estimates exact token-wise conditional log-likelihoods of the gated embeddings, while an auxiliary reconstruction head improves sensitivity to micro-level deviations that may be weakly reflected by NLL alone. On FT-AED, DA-GTNF achieves an AUC of 0.7218, a Reporting Delay of −11.80 min, a Mean Localization Error of 2.23 miles, and 100% incident coverage. On PeMS with incomplete ground truth, the segment-level DA-GTNF variant also consistently improves Recall@K% over all compared baselines.

source_records.abstract: Among various spatio-temporal prediction tasks, epidemic forecasting plays a critical role in public health management. Recent studies have demonstrated the strong potential of spatio-temporal graph neural networks in extracting heterogeneous spatio-temporal patterns for epidemic forecasting. However, most of these methods bear an oversimplified assumption that two locations (e.g., cities) with similar observed features in previous time steps will develop similar infection numbers in the future. In fact, for any epidemic disease, there exists strong heterogeneity of its latent transmission dynamics across both geolocation and time, which can eventually lead to diverged infection numbers in two “similar” locations. However, capturing such latent transmission heterogeneity is non-trivial due to the existence of numerous influencing factors like medical resource accessibility, virus mutations, mobility patterns, etc., most of which are spatio-temporal yet unreachable or even unobservable. To address this challenge, we propose a Heterogeneous Epidemic-Aware Transmission Graph Neural Network (HeatGNN), a novel epidemic forecasting framework. By integrating epidemiological modeling into a Graph Neural Network, HeatGNN learns epidemiology-informed location embeddings of different locations that reflect their own transmission dynamics over time. On top of the conventional spatio-temporal module, a heterogeneous transmission graph network is designed to uncover the latent transmission heterogeneity among locations, where the time-varying latent transmission affinity graphs are computed on-the-fly and provide additional predictive signals. Experiments (Code is available at https://github.com/YufanZheng/HeatGNN_ECML-PKDD .) on four benchmark datasets have revealed that HeatGNN outperforms various strong baselines.

source_records.abstract: With the rapid development of IoT technologies and widespread deployment of intelligent sensing devices, dynamic sensor selection has become crucial for balancing recognition accuracy and energy efficiency in applications like health monitoring. Existing runtime assessment methods suffer from limited predictive utility for future sensor quality and fail to capture dynamic spatio-temporal dependencies among interconnected devices. To this end, we propose a utility-aware sensor selection framework that integrates adaptive spatio-temporal forecasting with attention-based quality assessment. Our approach employs a Dynamic Graph Learning-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (DGL-STGCN) to model evolving device correlations and predict sensor states, while an attention mechanism assesses future sensor utility through learned importance scores. This enables proactive sensor selection optimized for both recognition accuracy and energy consumption, explicitly accounting for switching overheads. We develop and evaluate a prototype system designed for wearable devices to monitor locomotion activities. Results show that our system achieves a 14% accuracy improvement over single-sensor baselines, a 25% reduction in energy consumption compared to full-sensor deployment, and a 2% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at equivalent energy levels.

source_records.abstract: Accurate traffic forecasting requires effective modeling of complex spatio-temporal dependencies and reliable uncertainty estimation. Although existing graph-based methods have achieved strong performance, most focus on deterministic prediction and do not explicitly incorporate structural information into probabilistic modeling. In this paper, we propose HBPC-GWN, a hierarchical Bayesian calibration framework for graph-based traffic forecasting. Rather than imposing structural constraints during training, the proposed method performs posterior-level calibration by integrating a Laplacian-based prior into the predictive distribution. This enables a principled combination of data-driven predictions and graph-structured regularization, improving the consistency between spatial structure and uncertainty estimation. We instantiate the framework on Graph WaveNet and evaluate it on multiple real-world traffic datasets. Experimental results show that HBPC-GWN achieves competitive and more stable performance across forecasting horizons. In particular, it provides consistent improvements in medium- and long-term forecasting and improves probabilistic calibration, as reflected by better negative log-likelihood and prediction interval coverage. These results demonstrate that incorporating structural priors at the posterior level is an effective and flexible strategy for enhancing both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation in traffic forecasting.

source_records.abstract: Accurate forecasting of electric vehicle (EV) charging demand is essential for maintaining power-grid stability and supporting the efficient operation of urban charging infrastructure. However, EV charging demand exhibits strong spatio-temporal heterogeneity, multi-scale fluctuations, and complex dependencies, making accurate forecasting challenging. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-informed spatio-temporal graph learning framework for EV charging demand forecasting. Specifically, PSO-optimized MVMD is used to reconstruct multi-regional occupancy sequences, while a 2D-CNN is employed to capture temporal interaction patterns between occupancy and electricity price. A GAT-GFC-BiGRU-TPA architecture is then developed to model spatial dependencies and key temporal dynamics across charging regions. In addition, a physics-informed meta-learning strategy with a price-sensitivity regularization term is introduced to better capture the demand-response relationship between charging demand and electricity price while improving cross-region adaptability and training stability. Experiments on a real-world EV charging dataset show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple forecasting horizons. Ablation studies further verify the effectiveness of the major components. Overall, the proposed framework effectively captures complex spatio-temporal dynamics and improves short- and medium-term EV charging demand forecasting.

source_records.abstract: Multi-type epileptiform events, including spike and ripple activities in electroencephalogram (EEG), are important biomarkers for seizure detection; however, their accurate detection is challenging due to complex spatio-temporal dynamics and multi-scale oscillatory patterns. To address these challenges, we propose a unified framework that integrates clinically motivated multi-band decomposition with dynamic spatio-temporal representation learning for accurate classification of EEG signals. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into multiple frequency branches, followed by a branch-aware wavelet enhancement module to emphasize transient oscillatory patterns. A multi-scale temporal convolution module is then employed to capture diverse temporal dynamics across different time scales. Finally, a dynamic spatio-temporal graph reasoning module constructs sample-adaptive spatial and temporal graphs and performs joint propagation to model inter-channel interactions and temporal dependencies. Extensive experiments conducted on both a private clinical dataset and the public TUEV dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in epileptic event detection. These results highlight its effectiveness in capturing clinically relevant EEG patterns and its potential for assisting automated epilepsy diagnosis.

source_records.abstract: Among various spatio-temporal prediction tasks, epidemic forecasting plays a critical role in public health management. Recent studies have demonstrated the strong potential of spatio-temporal graph neural networks in extracting heterogeneous spatio-temporal patterns for epidemic forecasting. However, most of these methods bear an oversimplified assumption that two locations (e.g., cities) with similar observed features in previous time steps will develop similar infection numbers in the future. In fact, for any epidemic disease, there exists strong heterogeneity of its latent transmission dynamics across both geolocation and time, which can eventually lead to diverged infection numbers in two “similar” locations. However, capturing such latent transmission heterogeneity is non-trivial due to the existence of numerous influencing factors like medical resource accessibility, virus mutations, mobility patterns, etc., most of which are spatio-temporal yet unreachable or even unobservable. To address this challenge, we propose a Heterogeneous Epidemic-Aware Transmission Graph Neural Network (HeatGNN), a novel epidemic forecasting framework. By integrating epidemiological modeling into a Graph Neural Network, HeatGNN learns epidemiology-informed location embeddings of different locations that reflect their own transmission dynamics over time. On top of the conventional spatio-temporal module, a heterogeneous transmission graph network is designed to uncover the latent transmission heterogeneity among locations, where the time-varying latent transmission affinity graphs are computed on-the-fly and provide additional predictive signals. Experiments (Code is available at https://github.com/YufanZheng/HeatGNN_ECML-PKDD .) on four benchmark datasets have revealed that HeatGNN outperforms various strong baselines.

source_records.abstract: With the rapid development of IoT technologies and widespread deployment of intelligent sensing devices, dynamic sensor selection has become crucial for balancing recognition accuracy and energy efficiency in applications like health monitoring. Existing runtime assessment methods suffer from limited predictive utility for future sensor quality and fail to capture dynamic spatio-temporal dependencies among interconnected devices. To this end, we propose a utility-aware sensor selection framework that integrates adaptive spatio-temporal forecasting with attention-based quality assessment. Our approach employs a Dynamic Graph Learning-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (DGL-STGCN) to model evolving device correlations and predict sensor states, while an attention mechanism assesses future sensor utility through learned importance scores. This enables proactive sensor selection optimized for both recognition accuracy and energy consumption, explicitly accounting for switching overheads. We develop and evaluate a prototype system designed for wearable devices to monitor locomotion activities. Results show that our system achieves a 14% accuracy improvement over single-sensor baselines, a 25% reduction in energy consumption compared to full-sensor deployment, and a 2% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at equivalent energy levels.

source_records.abstract: Accurate traffic forecasting requires effective modeling of complex spatio-temporal dependencies and reliable uncertainty estimation. Although existing graph-based methods have achieved strong performance, most focus on deterministic prediction and do not explicitly incorporate structural information into probabilistic modeling. In this paper, we propose HBPC-GWN, a hierarchical Bayesian calibration framework for graph-based traffic forecasting. Rather than imposing structural constraints during training, the proposed method performs posterior-level calibration by integrating a Laplacian-based prior into the predictive distribution. This enables a principled combination of data-driven predictions and graph-structured regularization, improving the consistency between spatial structure and uncertainty estimation. We instantiate the framework on Graph WaveNet and evaluate it on multiple real-world traffic datasets. Experimental results show that HBPC-GWN achieves competitive and more stable performance across forecasting horizons. In particular, it provides consistent improvements in medium- and long-term forecasting and improves probabilistic calibration, as reflected by better negative log-likelihood and prediction interval coverage. These results demonstrate that incorporating structural priors at the posterior level is an effective and flexible strategy for enhancing both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation in traffic forecasting.

source_records.abstract: Accurate forecasting of electric vehicle (EV) charging demand is essential for maintaining power-grid stability and supporting the efficient operation of urban charging infrastructure. However, EV charging demand exhibits strong spatio-temporal heterogeneity, multi-scale fluctuations, and complex dependencies, making accurate forecasting challenging. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-informed spatio-temporal graph learning framework for EV charging demand forecasting. Specifically, PSO-optimized MVMD is used to reconstruct multi-regional occupancy sequences, while a 2D-CNN is employed to capture temporal interaction patterns between occupancy and electricity price. A GAT-GFC-BiGRU-TPA architecture is then developed to model spatial dependencies and key temporal dynamics across charging regions. In addition, a physics-informed meta-learning strategy with a price-sensitivity regularization term is introduced to better capture the demand-response relationship between charging demand and electricity price while improving cross-region adaptability and training stability. Experiments on a real-world EV charging dataset show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple forecasting horizons. Ablation studies further verify the effectiveness of the major components. Overall, the proposed framework effectively captures complex spatio-temporal dynamics and improves short- and medium-term EV charging demand forecasting.

source_records.abstract: Multi-type epileptiform events, including spike and ripple activities in electroencephalogram (EEG), are important biomarkers for seizure detection; however, their accurate detection is challenging due to complex spatio-temporal dynamics and multi-scale oscillatory patterns. To address these challenges, we propose a unified framework that integrates clinically motivated multi-band decomposition with dynamic spatio-temporal representation learning for accurate classification of EEG signals. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into multiple frequency branches, followed by a branch-aware wavelet enhancement module to emphasize transient oscillatory patterns. A multi-scale temporal convolution module is then employed to capture diverse temporal dynamics across different time scales. Finally, a dynamic spatio-temporal graph reasoning module constructs sample-adaptive spatial and temporal graphs and performs joint propagation to model inter-channel interactions and temporal dependencies. Extensive experiments conducted on both a private clinical dataset and the public TUEV dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in epileptic event detection. These results highlight its effectiveness in capturing clinically relevant EEG patterns and its potential for assisting automated epilepsy diagnosis.

source_records.abstract: Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting still suffers from three linked limitations: balanced graph operators mismatch open road networks, sequence-style SSMs ignore real graph topology, and physics losses may become self-referential. We propose UOT-GraphSSM, which combines an unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) layer, a graph-native anisotropic SSM recurrence, and a stop-gradient CTM physics loss. The UOT layer produces a mass-relaxed asymmetric transport plan for directional boundary flux; the GraphSSM recurrence propagates hidden states along this plan rather than along a serialized node order; and the CTM loss provides non-circular physical regularisation. On PEMS04/07/08, UOT-GraphSSM achieves consistent state-of-the-art results, reducing MSE by 7–25%, lowering long-horizon degradation from 65% to 43%, and retaining a compact 1.6 M-parameter footprint.

source_records.abstract: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) commonly utilize attention mechanisms to capture spatio-temporal dependencies. However, these methods often derive attention weights based on feature similarity, leading to an insufficient utilization of explicit topological evolution signals. This limitation hinders the model’s ability to perceive distinct structural roles within evolving graphs. To address this issue, we introduce Knowledge-Enhanced Spatio-Temporal ModuleKESTM (KES TM), a unified framework that bridges lightweight structural priors with adaptive spatio-temporal attention. KESTM comprises three key components: (1) a Knowledge Enhancement Module (KEM) that encodes multi-scale degree statistics and structural embeddings into learnable node-level priors; (2) an Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Encoder (ASTE) that employs a dual-stream attention mechanism with sparsity-aware gating to dynamically balance structural and temporal signals; and (3) a Dynamic Temporal-Contrastive Loss (DTCL) that jointly handles class imbalance and temporal inconsistency. Extensive experiments on four real-world dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. In particular, KESTM shows significant robustness under extreme graph sparsity, effectively addressing the Sparsity-Performance Paradox. Code is available at https://github.com/tyut2018/KESTM .

read_results.text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of deep learning models that have demonstrated significant potential in various classification tasks, including image recognition and the prediction of labels for nodes and edges. Unlike traditional neural networks that operate on Euclidean data such as images or sequences, GNNs are specifically designed to handle non-Euclidean data, i.e. data represented as graphs, where relationships between entities are irregular and complex. These graphs may include rich node and edge attributes, making GNNs particularly suitable for domains such as social networks, molecular structures, and recommendation systems. Several GNN variants have been developed, including GCN, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAGE, and FastGCN. Despite their advantages, GNNs often require substantial memory, primarily due to the large adjacency matrices involved, which become computationally expensive for large-scale graphs. They also tend to have long training times. In this work, we propose a novel graph partitioning technique aimed at reducing the effective size of the graph while maintaining a high predictive F1-score. Furthermore, we integrate this partitioning approach with layer-wise training to enhance computational efficiency.

source_records.abstract: Large graphs can be considered to be made of small subgraphs, called graphlets , that make up its fundamental building blocks. Therefore, counting graphlet frequencies is valuable for understanding structural characteristics and function of a given graph. In this paper, we propose an efficient algorithm CaTSCAN for counting the exact frequencies of typed graphlets of size up to 5 nodes in heterogeneous information networks, where the nodes of the graph (and graphlets) are assigned different types. Existing work has only addressed simpler problems, either focused on counting untyped graphlets of sizes up to 5 nodes, or in the case of typed graphlets, only considered counting graphlets with 3 and 4 nodes. CaTSCAN avoids excessive enumeration of individual graphlet instances by deriving the counts of larger graphlets from smaller ones with non-trivial and highly efficient combinatorics, while preserving type information. In an experimental evaluation, we show that CaTSCAN outperforms existing typed graphlet solutions on real-world datasets by up to 4 orders of magnitude for counting 3- and 4-node graphlets, and counts 5-node graphlets in less time than existing solutions count 3- and 4-node graphlets. CaTSCAN can even out-speed some untyped baselines on larger graphs.

source_records.abstract: Temporal graphs are a variety of structured data that have been particularly studied recently. In this paper, we focus on classification of temporal graphs. Previous works have shown that such task can be tackled by first transforming temporal graphs to static ones using ad-hoc algorithms, before the classification step. However, resulting static graphs might be of huge size. Transitive reduction can be used to reduce the size and redundancy of such graphs, but with a high complexity time. In this paper, we propose a fully dynamic algorithm that transforms temporal graphs into static ones while applying exact transitive reduction at the same time. This algorithm has a much reduced complexity than doing both steps separately, while producing exactly the same output graphs. We show in the experimental section that similar accuracy is achieved for a lower computational time.

raw_metadata.abstract: Temporal graphs are a variety of structured data that have been particularly studied recently. In this paper, we focus on classification of temporal graphs. Previous works have shown that such task can be tackled by first transforming temporal graphs to static ones using ad-hoc algorithms, before the classification step. However, resulting static graphs might be of huge size. Transitive reduction can be used to reduce the size and redundancy of such graphs, but with a high complexity time. In this paper, we propose a fully dynamic algorithm that transforms temporal graphs into static ones while applying exact transitive reduction at the same time. This algorithm has a much reduced complexity than doing both steps separately, while producing exactly the same output graphs. We show in the experimental section that similar accuracy is achieved for a lower computational time.

source_records.abstract: Dynamic resource allocation represents one of the core benefits of server virtualisation. Within a cloud computing context, a user issues an infrastructure request, which is satisfied by spawning one or several virtual machines (VMs). We argue that tearing down VMs once the initial request completes can prove sub-optimal. Indeed, this implies that for every new infrastructure request, the VM creation procedure is applied and, therefore, incurs the VM creation overhead. In this reseach, we consider workload placement as the first response to an infrastructure request, followed by a VM placement when no running VM has the capacity to execute the workload. Our solution proposes a multi-heuristic approach to workload placement in VMs. First, we employ a compound scoring function in the vector bin packing (VBP) algorithm to optimally assign workloads to running VMs. Next, the remaining workloads are placed on available VMs using a beam search (BS)-flavoured ant colony optimisation (ACO). We present an empirical evaluation with varied configurations to demonstrate that coupling VBP and ACO enhances the placement quality.

source_records.abstract: Timeline summarization aims to condense evolving information across multiple documents into coherent chronological narratives. In the sports domain, this task is particularly challenging due to the volume of news and the need to focus on user-preferred attributes such as specific players or teams. While prior work has explored generic timeline summarization, datasets supporting attribute-aware timeline summarization in sports remain limited. To address this, we introduce MulSports , a dataset designed to facilitate research on attribute-conditioned timeline summarization for sports news. MulSports comprises 2,000 news articles spanning football, cricket, kabaddi, hockey, and volleyball, paired with extracted player and team attributes and human-written timeline summaries. Each instance associates temporally ordered articles with a target attribute, enabling evaluation of both attribute focus and temporal coherence. To illustrate the utility of MulSports , we present an empirical analysis using a simple multi-modular pipeline that integrates temporal retrieval with large language models. Experimental results show that fine-tuned models outperform prompt-based baselines. MulSports provides a foundation for studying personalized and temporally grounded summarization in sports. The code, datasets, and Appendix material are made available through an anonymous GitHub repository ( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TimeAgent-277B/ ).

source_records.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of deep learning models that have demonstrated significant potential in various classification tasks, including image recognition and the prediction of labels for nodes and edges. Unlike traditional neural networks that operate on Euclidean data such as images or sequences, GNNs are specifically designed to handle non-Euclidean data, i.e. data represented as graphs, where relationships between entities are irregular and complex. These graphs may include rich node and edge attributes, making GNNs particularly suitable for domains such as social networks, molecular structures, and recommendation systems. Several GNN variants have been developed, including GCN, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAGE, and FastGCN. Despite their advantages, GNNs often require substantial memory, primarily due to the large adjacency matrices involved, which become computationally expensive for large-scale graphs. They also tend to have long training times. In this work, we propose a novel graph partitioning technique aimed at reducing the effective size of the graph while maintaining a high predictive F1-score. Furthermore, we integrate this partitioning approach with layer-wise training to enhance computational efficiency.

source_records.abstract: This study presents an extension of the conventional data warehouse query paradigm by introducing Multi-dimensional Graph eXpression (MGX), a multidimensional query framework designed to support Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) over graph-based business intelligence data. MGX extends the traditional Multi-Dimensional eXpression (MDX) syntax used in relational data warehouses by incorporating SQL-style analytical constructs, including GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY, thereby improving the expressive capability and flexibility of multidimensional analysis over graph warehouses. By bridging relational data warehousing technologies with graph-based analytical environments, the proposed framework addresses key limitations of traditional MDX in supporting graph-oriented analytics. It enables more effective exploration of semantically rich and socially connected knowledge embedded in networked datasets. Overall, MGX provides a practical methodological foundation for advancing graph warehousing and supporting next-generation network-centric business intelligence applications.

source_records.abstract: Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) often cause significant adverse events, making early identification crucial, especially with rising polypharmacy. While most methods focus on binary prediction, multiclass DDI prediction is more advantageous as it identifies specific interaction types. However, this is challenging due to class imbalance, with many rare interaction types compared to dominant ones. We propose a multiclass DDI prediction framework comprising three components: Stage 1 involves feature extraction, where the molecular structures of two drugs are modeled as graphs using a graph attention network (GAT) as an encoder, then combined with Drug Repurposing Knowledge Graph (DRKG) embeddings to produce enhanced drug features. Stage 2 involves expert modelling, where the paired drug representations are processed by two Mamba State Space Model (SSM)- based experts: a standard Mamba expert and a class-reweighted Mamba expert, which efficiently capture sequential dependencies and interaction patterns between the drug representations. Stage 3 involves gated fusion, where a confidence-based gating strategy integrates the two experts to generate final predictions. The performance on DrugBank and DDIMDL benchmark datasets achieved macro F1 scores of 90.68% and 83.99%, demonstrating our framework’s effectiveness in multiclass DDI prediction. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/devalab/MambaDDI .

source_records.abstract: Recent progress in fMRI-based visual brain decoding has enabled the reconstruction of neural visual signals as high-quality images using diffusion-based generative models. However, evaluating the semantic fidelity of these reconstructions remains challenging. Existing metrics, primarily based on pixel-level similarity or global embeddings, fail to capture the saliency-driven, structural, and relational aspects central to human scene understanding. We propose a saliency-aware, graph-based similarity metric, SSG, that compares stimuli and reconstructions through compact semantic scene graphs centered on the most salient objects and their relationships. By integrating visual saliency, language-guided scene understanding, and instance-level grounding, our method produces weighted graph representations that emphasize meaningful content while suppressing background clutter. Reconstruction quality is assessed via saliency-weighted object and relation conformity, yielding an interpretable structural score aligned with human perceptual judgment. Experiments show that the proposed metric provides a more informative evaluation of visual brain reconstructions than existing alternatives and offers diagnostic insights that can guide reconstruction refinement.

Abstract

Abstract Temporal networks have gained significant prominence in the past decade for modelling dynamic interactions within complex systems. A key challenge in this domain is Temporal Link Prediction (TLP), which aims to forecast future connections by analysing historical network structures across a range of applications. While existing surveys have addressed specific aspects of TLP, they typically lack a comprehensive framework that distinguishes between representation and inference methods, the two key ingredients of TLP. This survey bridges this gap by introducing a novel taxonomy that explicitly examines representation and inference in existing methods, providing a novel classification of approaches for TLP. We analyse how different representation techniques capture temporal and structural dynamics, examining their compatibility with various inference methods for link prediction tasks. Our taxonomy not only clarifies the methodological landscape but also reveals promising unexplored combinations of existing techniques. This taxonomy provides a systematic foundation for tackling emerging challenges in TLP, including model explainability and scalable architectures for complex temporal networks.

Body

Introduction A temporal network is a network whose structure and properties evolve over time. In the past decade, temporal networks have been used to model interactions between the components of complex systems with dynamic structures and characteristics. A temporal network consists of two key elements: a set of nodes representing components of a system and a set of links indicating interactions between pairs of nodes. In temporal networks, links between nodes may appear or disappear over time, and new nodes may also join. Broadly, temporal networks are represented in two paradigms: snapshot-based and continuous-time (event-based). Snapshot-based networks discretise time into intervals, yielding a sequence of static graphs, which is intuitive but may lose fine-grained temporal information. In contrast, continuous-time networks preserve the exact timestamps of interactions (events), enabling models to capture dynamics at arbitrary resolutions [ 1 , 2 ]. This distinction forms the foundation for most temporal representation learning approaches and is particularly relevant to temporal link prediction (TLP). Identifying the likelihood of connecting between nodes to predict future links in a network (link prediction) is a fundamental problem that can be applied to various domains such as social networks [ 3 ], telecommunication networks [ 4 ], traffic forecasting [ 5 , 6 ] or knowledge graphs [ 7 , 8 ]. Link prediction was first discussed in the context of static networks [ 9 ] where the aim has been to predict future links based on a network’s current state. In this paper this is referred to as traditional link prediction. However, TLP uses a network’s historical states to predict the likelihood of future links. Incorporating historical dynamics into the TLP problem introduces additional complexity [ 10 , 11 ]. In social networks for instance, such as the one shown in Fig. 1 , the TLP task is to predict the likelihood of a future link between User 1 and User 3 based on the observed temporal interactions among users. Fig. 1 Temporal link prediction in a social network Recently, numerous methods have been proposed to address the TLP problem, each method focusing on different network characteristics. Solving TLP requires two key ingredients: first, a representation unit , which models how a temporal network can be captured to reflect its traits and historical dynamics; and second, an inference unit , which determines the likelihood of future links based on the learned representation. Since all TLP models necessarily need both units, this review is confined to approaches concerning either representation or inference. Traditional surveys often categorise TLP models into broad methodological families such as “learning-based” [ 11 ]. This perspective provides a useful overview of existing approaches, but tends to emphasise overall model families rather than disentangling specific design choices. For instance, both TGN [ 1 ] and EvolveGCN [ 12 ] are typically labelled as “learning-based,” yet their underlying assumptions differ markedly: TGN employs a continuous-time message passing representation units with attention-based units making it effective for modelling of rapidly evolving interactions, whereas EvolveGCN adopts a sequence of discrete snapshots with RNN-based updates of GCN parameters, which is more suitable for gradually evolving networks. In the paper, TLP models are classified according to whether their primary contribution is to representation or inference; the defining attributes in each unit form the basis for the taxonomy adopted here. By separating representation and inference units, our taxonomy highlights such distinctions more explicitly, thereby clarifying how models align with different data characteristics and task requirements, and revealing unexplored combinations. The survey begins by examining various representation methods and discusses their merits and challenges. It then classifies and evaluates the inference approaches that have been explored in the literature. Guided by this methodological perspective, the discussion is subsequently divided into two sections “ Review of Representation Units for TLP ” and “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ” dedicated to each unit, respectively. The survey highlights potential research opportunities through two primary avenues: (i) unexplored combinations of existing representation and inference units and (ii) the development of novel unit designs that could introduce new computational paradigms for either representation or inference. These opportunities could lead to more effective TLP approaches. Various surveys have been conducted to review TLP studies. Some surveys concentrate on specific network structures, such as homogeneous networks [ 13 , 14 ], or directed networks [ 15 ]. Other surveys focus on the application of TLP across various domains, encompassing temporal knowledge graphs [ 16 ] and social networks [ 3 , 17 , 18 ]. Our survey sets itself apart in several aspects: The survey introduces a novel taxonomy that distinguishes between the representation and inference units. Unlike existing surveys [ 13 , 14 – 15 ] which classify models under a single hierarchical framework, our approach separates these components to provide deeper insights into the models’ applicability and performance variations whilst also exploring diverse network characteristics pertinent to the TLP problem. The survey provides a comprehensive review of the representation unit. While previous surveys [ 3 , 17 ] provided some discussions of these models, we offer a systematic classification and analyse their ability to capture temporal and structural dynamics, thereby addressing a significant gap in the literature. The survey identifies current challenges and outlines potential directions for future research in representations, network characteristics, and TLP methodologies, offering valuable guidance for subsequent investigations in this field. Methods included in this survey come from papers identified using Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar and keywords on temporal networks, network representation and link prediction. Only articles written in English in the period 2000–2025 that propose relevant algorithms or methods were considered. The rest of this paper is organised as shown in Fig. 2 . “ Background ” presents the background on temporal graph representation and the problem statements. Following this, “ Taxonomy ” introduces the taxonomy framework. “ Review of Representation Units for TLP ” and “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ” provide an overview of TLP methods, classifying them based on their representation and inference units. “ Variations of the TLP Problem ” and “ Future Research D

irections ” explore variations of the TLP problem and outline potential directions for future research. Finally, “ Conclusion ” presents the survey’s conclusion. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a powerful framework for analyzing structured data in the form of graphs, with applications spanning diverse fields such as social networks, biology, and recommender systems. This survey explores methodology, development, and advances in GNN architecture. We methodically survey the major classes of GNNs, including convolutional GNNs (ConvGNNs), spatial–temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs), recurrent-based GNNs (RecGNNs), and graph autoencoders (GAEs). Every model is discussed in terms of underlying mathematical formulations, design principles, and practical applications. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of GNNs for practitioners, students, and researchers alike, highlighting their versatility and potential for future innovations in graph neural networks. This review is broad, addressing the basic ideas behind GNNs, different architectural designs, training and inference methods, common issues and constraints, the variety of datasets used, and real-world applications across numerous fields. We will furthermore discuss applications of graph neural networks across different fields and exemplify open-source codes, benchmark datasets, and model valuation for graph neural networks. In the end, this survey specifies existing challenges in interpretability, generalization, and scalability and proposes possible future research trends to further promote the performance of GNNs across various graph-based learning missions.

Graphs has been a ubiquitous way of representing heterogeneous data. There are many studies focused on graph learning highlighting the approaches for graph data extraction, interpretation and graph summarization. Graph data summarization is achieving more expansion due to the broader length of sizeable applications and interpretation of proper understanding about the hidden details of the data using deep learning-based graph representation. Graph interpretation and summarization have come up as an interdisciplinary room that has vividly broader influence over multiple parallel areas and real-world applications. In other words, extraction of relevant data from massive and complex graph structure, enables the data to be used by many application area. However, it is found that recognizing the discriminatory and hidden properties from massive heterogeneous data is not easy in case of both nodal graph and graph image (also known as chart image). Hence, deep learning based approaches eventuated as a satisfactory solution. This paper presents an outline of the quantitative and statistical approaches used for learning and understanding different integrant of nodal graph and information graph, such as data extraction and processing, interpretation, summarization and visualization, by using graph-based learning methods. These integrant are broadly considered under (or as) SIV Model in this paper. Paper also discusses the influence of summarization techniques on the visualization of large data graphs and upcoming research areas of summarization. Lastly, paper provides with brief overview of challenges, application area, benefits of graph interpretation, summarization, and visualization, while providing existing tools and datasets available for graph processing and learning.

With the rise of large-scale social networks, network mining has become an important sub-domain of data mining. Generating an efficient network representation is one important challenge in applying machine learning to network data. Recently, representation learning methods are widely used in various domains to generate low dimensional latent features from complex high dimensional data. A significant amount of research effort is made in the past few years to generate node representations from graph-structured data using representation learning methods. Here, we provide a detailed study of the latest advancements in the field of network representation learning (also called network embedding). We first discuss the basic concepts and models of network embedding. Further, we build a taxonomy of network embedding methods based on the type of networks and review the major research works that come under each category. We then cover the major datasets used in network embedding research and describe the major applications of network embedding with respect to various network mining tasks. Finally, we provide various directions for future work which enhance further research.

Summary This section introduced the foundations of temporal networks and the problem formulation of TLP. Temporal networks are modelled as temporal graphs, where the evolution of nodes, edges, and attributes can be described in either discrete-time or continuous-time paradigms, each offering different trade-offs between efficiency and information preservation. TLP extends traditional link prediction by requiring models to capture both spatial and temporal dynamics for forecasting future interactions. We further distinguished between transductive and inductive inference tasks, highlighting their respective assumptions and generalisation scopes. Overall, this background sets the stage for understanding the methodological developments reviewed in the following sections. In particular, the distinction between discrete-time and continuous-time representations, as well as between transductive and inductive inference tasks, provides the foundation for the taxonomy that follows. Taxonomy The Framework of the Taxonomy This survey proposes a taxonomy framework for TLP. It contends that all TLP methods comprise two sub-tasks: representing temporal networks and making predictions, which are processed by two distinct components: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The representation unit captures the network structure and dynamics, whilst the inference unit leverages these representations to forecast future links. As depicted in Fig. 5 a, nodes, edges, and attributes are processed by a representation unit to produce inputs that capture dynamic patterns. Subsequently, the inference units process features or embeddings derived from the representation unit to infer future links. In [ 26 ], transductive and inductive tasks relate to inference units but not to graph representation. Fig. 5 The framework of the taxonomy This survey categorises TLP methods based on their underlying elements, despite many approaches being hybrid, combining different representation and inference units or integrating general machine learning strategies. Figure 5 a shows that each method incorporates at least one representation unit and one inference unit. Since temporal networks can be modelled as either discrete-time or continuous-time dynamic graphs, and TLP tasks can be either transductive or inductive, methodologies are classified into four distinct categories based on these combinations, as illustrated in Fig. 5 b. The representation unit fundamentally encapsulates the spatial dynamics within the temporal networks. Inference units are the methods employed to process graph representations derived from representation units and learn dynamic patterns of temporal networks for TLP. Direct inference is a prevalent approach in representation unit applications, whereby embeddings or features from dynamic network embedding methods directly yield predictions without requiring additional model training. Techniques such as Euclidean Distance or adjacent matrix transformations are commonly employed. The method’s straightforward nature makes it particularly popular for one-step tasks. Moreover, it is important to highlight that several inference methods, including RNN-based and attention-based models, initially designed for inductive tasks, can effectively handle transductive tasks. This shows the adaptability of these models and suggests the potential for their broader application in different TLP scenarios. Table 2 summarises all the methods of inference units which are elaborated in “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ”. Relationship of Representation Unit and Inference Unit As illustrated in Fig. 5 a, data are first transformed by the Representation Unit into features or embeddings that capture structural and temporal dynamics. These representations are then processed by the Inference Unit to produce link predictions, often in conjunction with auxiliary components such as candidate generation or negative sampling [ 1 , 81 ]. A TLP model, therefore, relies on the alignment between the expressive capacity of its Representation Unit and the predictive capability of its Inference Unit. For example, simple feature extraction in the Representation Unit, such as similarity or centrality measures, is typically paired with lightweight inference techniques such as time series models or distance-based scoring. In contrast, latent states derived from graph neural network encoders or continuous-time event-driven models usually require parametric inference modules, including multilayer perceptrons, recurrent decoders, or attention-based predictors. It is also important to note that many approaches to Representation Units and Inference Units are rooted in neural network architectures. Graph neural networks, recurrent networks, and attention mechanisms are different forms of neural computation that can be employed in either stage. Consequently, TLP models of

ten integrate these components in diverse ways, combining representation and inference modules into flexible and powerful end-to-end architectures. This neural foundation provides both strong approximation ability and architectural adaptability, allowing researchers to design models that are tailored to specific temporal settings while retaining the capacity to generalise across a wide range of prediction tasks. Temporal Graph Benchmarks In recent years, significant progress has been made toward standardising evaluation in temporal graph link prediction, most notably through the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) [ 82 ] and its extension TGB 2.0 [ 83 ] on multi-relational and heterogeneous temporal graphs. These benchmarks provide datasets, unified preprocessing pipelines, and public leaderboards, 1 enabling systematic comparisons among a wide range of methods. TGB includes datasets from diverse domains. For example, a dataset on Wikipedia co-editing interactions focuses on predicting which page a user will edit at a given time [ 84 ]. Another dataset on Amazon product reviews considers the task of predicting the next product a user will review [ 85 ]. A financial dataset based on stablecoin ERC20 transactions requires forecasting the destination address of a transfer, including cases during the Terra Luna collapse [ 86 ]. A social media dataset constructed from Reddit reply dynamics predicts whether one user will respond to another [ 87 ]. Finally, a dataset on international flights predicts whether a flight will occur between two airports on a specified day [ 88 ]. Collectively, these datasets span domains such as collaborative editing, e-commerce, finance, social media, and transportation, highlighting the broad range of real-world applications for TLP. Both TGB and TGB 2.0 report systematic comparisons of TLP methods, ranging from classical heuristics and static baselines to state-of-the-art temporal graph neural networks such as JODIE, TGN, and CAW. The leaderboard results highlight that while sophisticated temporal models often achieve strong predictive performance, simple memory-based heuristics also remain competitive, especially on large-scale datasets. Summary Building on the distinctions introduced in the previous section, this taxonomy frames TLP methods around two complementary units: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The Representation Unit reflects the discrete-time vs continuous-time modelling paradigm, focusing on how temporal networks are represented and encoded. The Inference Unit corresponds to the transductive vs inductive inference setting, determining how predictions are carried out given the learned representations. By combining these two dimensions, we categorise existing methods into four principal groups, providing a coherent structure for understanding these approaches. This design not only ensures consistency with the conceptual foundations of temporal networks but also highlights open challenges, such as bridging hybrid Representation and Inference Units, balancing representational fidelity and efficiency, and enabling models to generalise across diverse TLP scenarios. Review of Representation Units for TLP Discrete-time Dynamic Graphs Methods Snapshots The Snapshots approach is a fundamental method employed in the domain of discrete-time dynamic graphs for TLP. This technique directly inputs network temporal adjacency matrices into the inference unit. The snapshots are treated as a sequence of static networks and are structurally represented by adjacency matrices. This method is effective for tasks that resemble time-series inference. The direct use of snapshots simplifies the representation and processing of dynamic graphs, making it an efficient choice for many application scenarios. Building on this observation, researchers have developed neighbour-based methods that utilise neighbourhood topological information from discrete snapshots for TLP.
